I signed up for HeyGen using my personal email because I wanted to evaluate the platform before potentially introducing it to my company for creating professional training videos.

Initially, I thought the subscription pricing was very reasonable. Cost was never my concern. I was willing to pay for a quality product.

Unfortunately, the experience quickly became frustrating. While producing a 36-minute training video, I was repeatedly notified that I needed to purchase additional credits to continue. Each time I purchased more credits, I was told I still didn't have enough. This happened multiple times until I had spent approximately $250.

Even at that price, I would have been satisfied if the final product had turned out well.

I invested considerable time writing scripts, organizing content, and following HeyGen's instructions. Unfortunately, I couldn't properly preview the finished video before committing to the additional charges.

Once the video was generated, I had to split it into separate segments and use third-party software to stitch everything together. That was inconvenient, but manageable.

The real problem came when I reviewed the final video and discovered sections displaying completely white screens instead of the intended content. These appeared to be rendering issues, despite my having followed the instructions carefully.

When I attempted to troubleshoot and correct the problems, I was once again prompted to purchase additional credits!

To make matters worse, the AI-powered customer support was extremely disappointing and failed to provide a meaningful resolution.

My biggest frustration is that customers should not have to keep paying to correct technical problems with a product they've already paid to generate.

As a business professional evaluating this platform for potential company use, this experience completely destroyed my confidence in HeyGen. I canceled my subscription and decided to look elsewhere for our AI training video needs.

What could have been an opportunity to gain a business customer turned into a very disappointing experience.

Bottom line: I have no problem paying for quality. I do have a problem being repeatedly charged for a product that ultimately proved unusable, with little meaningful support to resolve the issues.

I cannot recommend HeyGen based on my experience.

I'm a heavy HeyGen user. I bought 50,000 credits to translate an online course into 10 languages. While testing my voice in different languages, voice previews were suddenly blocked, with no warning and no information anywhere in the platform about a preview limit.

What followed was the worst support experience I've had with a paid tool:

The AI assistant said the block would "probably" last 24 hours, but could be 30 days.
Support L1 told me it would "automatically reset 24 hours after it was triggered" and to "rest assured that it will expire on said time."
Advanced Support then said it would only come back two weeks later, on October 28, and that the limit was part of my Pro plan.
Then they said it has nothing to do with my plan and won't reset on my renewal date (October 19), because it runs on a separate cycle that isn't shown anywhere in my account.

When I asked for a solution, I got a one-line apology and an offer to upgrade to Enterprise at $25,000/year. No reset, no compensation.

The product itself is good, but the limits are hidden, the support doesn't know its own rules, and the answer to a customer who invests heavily in the platform is "pay more." If you plan to produce at scale, be very careful.

However, the editing experience has been incredibly frustrating and expensive.  
I have 8 modules with roughly 4 to 5 lessons each, so I need a reliable way to make small scene corrections. In one video, I needed just one scene changed. I gave HeyGen an exact reference image, very specific instructions, and clearly stated which scene needed to be replaced.  
HeyGen told me four separate times that the scene had been updated and was ready for review. Each time, I checked the video and the scene had not been changed.  
When I pointed this out, HeyGen would respond that I was correct, apologize, and acknowledge that it had not actually made the change. Then it would tell me it would fix it, only to repeat the same problem again.  
On another attempt, instead of changing the scene I requested, it changed the wrong scene entirely.  
It ultimately took five attempts to correct one scene.  
The biggest issue is not simply that AI sometimes makes mistakes. The issue is that HeyGen repeatedly told me the requested edit had been completed when it had not. That caused me to keep retrying and spending valuable credits based on inaccurate confirmations from the system.  
I have more than 40 lessons in this course. I cannot spend hours fighting with the platform and burning credits every time one scene needs a minor correction.  
It is disappointing because I truly do love the quality of many of the videos HeyGen produced. If the editing process were reliable, I would happily continue using it. But at this point, the repeated failed edits, incorrect confirmations, and unnecessary credit usage have made the platform too unreliable and expensive for a project of this size.

We've been using Synthesia to create educational videos for our students, and from a product perspective it's excellent. The quality of the AI avatars, voices and overall platform has been a great asset to our business.

Unfortunately, our experience with the monthly subscription model has been disappointing.

Our plan includes a monthly allocation of credits. The issue is that if you don't have enough credits remaining to generate a complete video, those credits become effectively unusable. At the end of the billing cycle, any unused credits are simply wiped, despite having been paid for.

When we raised this with customer support, we were told to "make sure you use all your credits" or switch to an annual subscription. Unfortunately, that isn't a practical solution. If the remaining balance isn't enough to create another video, there is no way to use those credits before they expire.

We have no objection to paying a premium for a month-to-month subscription. We simply believe customers should receive fair value for what they've paid for. Allowing a limited credit rollover, the ability to purchase only the shortfall required to complete a video, or even a small overdraft deducted from the following month's credits would solve this issue and demonstrate a more customer-focused approach.

We genuinely like the product and would happily continue using it long-term. However, the current credit policy leaves us feeling that we've paid for something we are not given a fair opportunity to use, which is disappointing for an otherwise outstanding platform.

In many cases, I find myself repeatedly refreshing the voice output in an attempt to produce something usable, and at times I have abandoned projects entirely due to these limitations.

HeyGen (and our V1 model) literally uses the user on-boarding video in the final output. See here for a demonstration of this (https://toinfinityai.github.io/v2-launch-page/#comparisons). We are not talking about that in this thread. We are trying to solve a quirk of our Diffusion Transformer model (V2 model).

Our V2 model is trained on specific durations of audio (2s, 5s, 10s, etc) as input. So, if give the model a 7s audio clip during inference, it will generate lower quality videos than at 5s or 10s. So, instead, we buffer the audio to the nearest training bucket (10s in this case). We have tried buffering it with a zero array, white noise and just concatenating the input audio (inverted) to the end. The drawback is that the last frame (the one at 7s) has a higher likelihood to fail. We need to solve this.

And, no shade on HeyGen. It's literally what we did before. And their videos look hyper realistic, which is great for B2B content. The drawback is you are always constrained to the hand motions and environment of the on-boarding video, which is more limiting for entertainment content.

For IoT sensors devices, they mainly have regular and frequent interval sampling that probably in the ranges of every seconds, minutes, hours, etc. Some if not most of this data is not clean data, there are raw data, and raw data is inherently big and huge compared to the data, for example raw image data vs JPEG data, where the former can be several time bigger in size and processing requirements.

Summary:

Two companies are profiled, Synthesia and Rosebud, that specialize in Machine Learning-supported video alteration.

They help their customers build videos where:

- The speaker uses different languages than the source recording

- Human avatars are generated from model captures, and these avatars will "read" scripts, without needing to put said human in front of the camera again.

- Current use is for PSAs, marketing videos, and training materials.

Here is a summary of potential mitigations for those too busy to click:

# Limiting users or use cases

- User Vetting: Carefully vet those who can use a tool (Example: Synthesia only working with vetted enterprise clients.)

- Usage Constraints: Limit the synthesis possibilities. (Example: Humen is providing only a limited set of movements for generated videos.)

# Discouraging malicious use of flexible and public tools

- Clear disclosure: Ensuring and requiring that manipulated outputs are clearly labeled (including via metadata).

- Consent protection: Requiring the consent of those being impersonated.

- Detection friendliness: Supporting those working on detection and not seeking to fool detection systems.

- Hidden watermarks: Embedding data through robust watermarks.

- Usage logs: Storing information about usage and media outputs.

- Use restrictions: Enforcing contracts that prohibit forms of violative or malicious use.

Not all apply to every system of course. The article has more detail!
